title: Bali
capsule: From the late seventeenth century until Dutch conquest in 1906–1908, Bali comprised a shifting constellation of Hindu kingdoms — Klungkung, Gianyar, Badung, Tabanan, Buleleng, Karangasem, Mengwi, and Bangli — that preserved a distinct Indic court culture long after Islam had spread across Java and Sumatra; the Dewa Agung at Klungkung held nominal paramount authority following the relocation of the Gelgel court there in 1686. Dutch colonial expansion absorbed Buleleng in 1849, Lombok and Karangasem in 1894, and southern Bali in 1906 after an expedition that prompted mass puputan (ritual self-destruction) by the courts of Badung and Tabanan. The final Dutch invasion of Klungkung in 1908 — again met with puputan by the Dewa Agung and his court — completed the conquest and incorporated Bali into the Netherlands East Indies.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The political structure of Balinese kingdoms is documented through Dutch colonial records and Balinese court chronicles (babad); representing the island as a single unified polity is a cartographic simplification, and internal borders between competing kingdoms are not precisely mappable.
